deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. Folio 76 is a fair copy of notes on ancient Greek history, continuing directly from folio 75 and into folio 77. The style suggests notes from a Göttingen lecture course on ancient history, of the kind A. H. L. Heeren gave; that attribution is my guess, not something the page states.

The content runs as follows:
(1) The Spartans arrived only after the battle of Marathon had already been won, dated 'c. 490. 29 Sept.'
(2) The victory raised Athenian morale. Athens wanted to punish those who had gone over to the Persian side. Miltiades was given a small fleet and brought several islands back under Athenian control.
(3) He failed at the siege of Paros, and a large part of the fleet was lost. He was blamed for the expedition and ordered to repay its costs. Unable to pay, he was imprisoned and died there.
(4) From here on Athenian history turns on the history of outstanding individuals. Miltiades' death made room for Themistocles and Aristides.
(5) Themistocles is described as the foremost talent of his time. He could conceive great plans and also carry them out, and he knew how to manage the people through their weaknesses. Athen owed to him (continued on f. 77) its development into a naval power.

There are no formulas, numbers or computations apart from the date 490 [BC], 29 September. The hand and subject matter make it uncertain whether the page is in Gauss's own hand or copied by someone else, for example a family member or student; I cannot settle this from the image. Either way, it has no mathematical content to reconstruct.
errors: Historical, not mathematical. The date '29 Sept.' for Marathon is the conventional date found in older handbooks. Later scholarship (e.g. Boeckh's lunar-calendar argument) usually puts it around 12 September 490 BC, or in August.

The statement that a large part of the fleet perished at Paros has no clear support in the ancient sources (Herodotus 6.132–136). Those sources stress the failed siege, Miltiades' leg wound, a fine of 50 talents, and his death from the wound. Death in prison is the version given by Nepos and some later writers.

results.what: Lecture-style narrative of Greek history: Marathon (490 BC), Miltiades' Paros expedition and death, characterization of Themistocles and Aristides
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th/early-19th-century Göttingen ancient-history curriculum (likely Heeren-type lectures; unsure)
